Peninsula cooter (Pseudemys peninsularis) hatchlings emerge from their leathery-shelled eggs with a carapace length at birth measuring approximately 2.5 centimeters [Lb = approximately 2.5 centimeters], a size that facilitates their early movement through the shallow, vegetated littoral zones of Florida's freshwater systems. This modest initial size permits neonates to exploit dense aquatic vegetation for shelter from predators shortly after eclosion. These hatchlings exhibit a rapid early growth phase, adding several millimeters to their carapace each month during their initial growing seasons. Individual growth trajectories, however, vary considerably depending on local resource availability and thermal conditions encountered within their specific aquatic habitats. The initial size at emergence represents a trade-off between maximizing clutch size and producing offspring large enough to avoid an extensive array of wading bird and fish predators. Over the course of their juvenile development, these turtles undergo substantial changes in both body dimensions and mass, gradually transitioning from a predominantly carnivorous diet to one that is largely herbivorous, a dietary shift that coincides with their increasing body size and changing metabolic demands.

Under controlled laboratory conditions designed to mimic the average summer water temperatures of their native habitat, female Peninsula cooters reach reproductive maturity after approximately 5 to 7 years since birth [tp = approximately 5 to 7 years since birth] when maintained at a constant 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This same thermal regime is associated with a maximum lifespan of 30 years [am = 30 years] in captivity, though wild individuals likely experience greater mortality pressures that may truncate their longevity at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. The attainment of puberty marks a critical transition in the life history of these turtles, as females must redirect a significant portion of their acquired energy from somatic growth toward the production of large, energy-rich eggs. The relatively slow maturation period is characteristic of many large-bodied emydid turtles and is linked to their delayed reproductive schedules and generally low annual adult mortality in stable environments. Males of this species, in contrast, attain sexual maturity at a noticeably younger age, requiring only about 3 to 4 years since birth [tp = about 3 to 4 years since birth] when exposed to the same consistent thermal cond at a temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]itions. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maturation timing likely reflects the different energetic demands imposed on males versus females during reproduction, with males needing only to achieve a size sufficient for successful courtship and copulation rather than for producing a large clutch of eggs.

Significant variation in maximum body size exists among populations of the Peninsula cooter, with some adult females achieving an ultimate carapace length of 33 centimeters [Li = 33 centimeters] in productive lake systems. In contrast, individuals occupying more resource-limited habitats, such as smaller ephemeral ponds, often cease growing at a much smaller adult size, with a documented ultimate carapace length for some populations being 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters]. This plasticity in final body size is a well-documented phenomenon among freshwater turtles and is primarily driven by differences in food availability, population density, and the length of the active growing season. The larger size attained in more productive environments likely confers advantages in terms of fecundity, as larger females can accommodate a greater number of eggs per clutch and may also experience lower predation rates due to their formidable shell dimensions. This intraspecific variation highlights the remarkable adaptability of this species to a wide range of ecological conditions across its peninsular range.

Adult females also demonstrate considerable intraspecific variation in their maximum wet body mass, ranging from a smaller morph that reaches an ultimate wet weight of 1800 grams [Wwi = 1800 grams] up to exceptionally large individuals that attain an ultimate wet weight of 6800 grams [Wwi = 6800 grams]. This fourfold difference in mass is among the largest recorded for any emydid turtle and reflects the species' occupation of a diverse array of habitats, from nutrient-poor oligotrophic lakes to highly productive eutrophic marshes. Heavier individuals are consistently found in habitats with abundant aquatic macrophytes, which form the bulk of the adult diet. The substantial investment in body mass by large females is directly linked to their reproductive output, as body volume constrains the physical space available for developing eggs. Heavier turtles also tend to have relatively larger body condition indices, suggestive of superior foraging success and habitat quality. These mass extremes document the outer limits of morphological variability present within this single, widespread species.

The reproductive output of the Peninsula cooter is seasonally concentrated, with females depositing approximately 11 to 16 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 11 to 16 eggs per clutch] during the late spring and early summer nesting season. A single female may deposit up to three such clutches within a single reproductive year [F_R_i = up to three such clutches within a single reproductive year] when water temperatures remain near 22 °C [T = 22 °C], a regime that optimizes both foraging efficiency and ovarian follicle development. The combination of a relatively large clutch size and a high annual clutch frequency results in a substantial per capita annual fecundity that helps offset the high rates of nest predation typically experienced in peninsular Florida. Eggs are deposited in flask-shaped nests excavated in sandy or loamy soils, often in open, well-drained areas adjacent to basking sites. Hatching success can be highly variable across years and is strongly influenced by seasonal rainfall patterns and the abundance of nest predators such as raccoons and fire ants. Females do not provide any parental care beyond nest site selection and burial.
